hero.title: Hi, I'm Wasif. I just wanted free storage
hero.subtext: Wasif Malik, or Wosmo to the internet. A full-stack engineer in Karachi, Pakistan who needed somewhere to put a lot of files, couldn't find storage that didn't also want to read them, and instead of letting it go like a reasonable person, spent a few months building his own. That's zcrypt. It's just me back here: no team, no investors, no “zcrypt family.” Which mostly means when something breaks, I already know whose fault it is.

trust.eyebrow: Why my name is on this
trust.body: A tool that holds your keys should at least tell you who to blame. So, that's me. Right here. There's no mysterious “we” to vanish behind when something breaks, no “the team is looking into it.” There is a team. It's me. The encryption runs on your device before anything uploads, so I can't read your files. I've tried it on my own test data. Can't. That's the entire point.

origin.heading: How zcrypt actually happened
origin.p1: A couple of months ago I was moving my whole life between machines: 50-something gigabytes of projects, RAW photos, and half-finished edits I keep swearing I'll get back to. The kind of files you can't just re-download.
origin.p2: Google Drive tapped me on the shoulder at 15GB and asked for my card. So I did the very reasonable thing: I made a second account. Then a third. For about a week I was splitting one folder across three logins like a low-budget digital smuggler, quietly proud of a system held together with tape.
origin.p3: Then I tried TeraBox. “One terabyte, free,” they said. What they didn't say: the download button is hidden like a state secret, your files quietly live on their servers, and the fine print treats your data as theirs to scan and learn from. It really clicked when I uploaded a 4GB folder, watched it crawl to 80%, and watched it fail. My first thought wasn't “let me retry.” It was “why am I handing my entire life to a company whose whole business is knowing what's inside it?”
origin.p4: And here's the part I genuinely can't take credit for, because it's just true: free storage was never free. I just hadn't read the price tag, because the price tag is me. These are billion-dollar companies; privacy isn't a feature they forgot to add, it's the thing they quietly sell against.
origin.p5: So I stopped complaining online and started building, which is really just complaining with extra steps. The idea was simple even though the code very much wasn't: encrypt your files on your device before they leave, so not even I can read them, then store them across the infrastructure you already own and trust. No new data empire. No “we value your privacy” banner that means the exact opposite. Just your files, locked, yours.
origin.pullQuote: Free storage was never free. I just hadn't read the price tag, because the price tag was me.
origin.after1: I'm building it in public: the wins, the bugs, and the 2AM “why is this WASM module re-initialising” commits. It's me and a concerning amount of coffee, so yes, there will be rough edges. The encryption isn't one of them: it's open source, and I can't read your files even if I wanted to. (I don't. But I couldn't.)
origin.philosophyLink: The longer, ranty version lives on the philosophy page

hero.title: Why we built zcrypt
hero.lede: A long-overdue conversation about who owns your data, who's profiting from it, and why that needs to change.

short.body: Most cloud storage means renting space on someone else's servers, where they hold the keys to your files. zcrypt is different. Your files are encrypted on your device, then stored inside free space you already have on accounts you own: GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, or Telegram. Only you can read them, you're limited only by your own storage, and it's free and open source.

rent.title: The cloud is just someone else's computer
rent.p1: And they're charging you rent to live in it.
rent.p2: Somewhere in the last decade, the tech industry pulled off one of history's great marketing tricks: they convinced billions of people to stop storing files on hardware they own and start paying monthly for the privilege of storing them on hardware that someone else owns.
rent.p3: This is the digital equivalent of renting a storage unit for things you already have room for at home. Except the storage unit also reads your mail, indexes your photo albums, and raises the rent every year.
rent.quote: Cloud storage is a landlord scheme with better PR.
rent.p4: AWS S3 charges $23 per terabyte per month. That's $276 per year for a terabyte of storage. A 4TB hard drive costs $80 on Amazon, the same Amazon. You could buy the physical hardware to store your data four times over for what they charge you in a single year to store it on their servers.
rent.p5: The markup isn't 100%. It isn't 500%. The markup on cloud storage is measured in thousands of percent, and the entire industry has collectively agreed to pretend this is normal.

loophole.title: Git storage, the loophole nobody talks about
loophole.p1: GitLab gives you 10GB per repo. For free. Hugging Face gives you 100GB per account. GitHub doesn't even publish a hard cap: just stay under a few gigabytes and nobody blinks. These aren't hidden terms buried in legalese, they're published limits (and unwritten norms) that platform teams actively maintain and support.
loophole.p2: This isn't a bug. This is a feature. These platforms need generous storage to host large repositories, ML models, and binary assets. They built the infrastructure. They set the limits. We just use them as intended, for storing data.
loophole.quote: Every terabyte we store for free is a terabyte AWS can't bill for.
loophole.p3: zcrypt takes your files, compresses them with Zstd, encrypts them with AES-256-GCM, splits them into manageable chunks, and stores them as ordinary-looking data in repositories on the platform you connect. To the platform, they look like build artifacts. To you, they're your encrypted files, accessible from anywhere, costing nothing.
loophole.p4: Is this safe and durable? Yes. Your data is stored as standard private repository content, exactly the kind of large binary data these platforms are built to host. zcrypt automatically spreads data across repositories and rotates to fresh ones as they fill up, so you stay well within each platform's normal limits. And your files are always retrievable: encrypted chunks are integrity-checked and reassembled when you download.

zk.title: Zero-knowledge is not a marketing buzzword
zk.p1: When Dropbox says “we take security seriously,” what they mean is they encrypt your files with keys they control. They can read your files. Their employees can read your files. They scan your files to build search indices. Government subpoenas? They hand over your data because they can.
zk.p2: When we say “zero-knowledge,” we mean the mathematical kind. Your passphrase never leaves your device. We derive encryption keys locally using PBKDF2 with 600,000 iterations. The encrypted data that gets uploaded is indistinguishable from random noise.
zk.quote: We can't read your files. Not because we're polite. Because we literally don't have the keys.
zk.p3: AES-256-GCM provides authenticated encryption, meaning tampering with the ciphertext is detectable. The GCM mode gives you both confidentiality and integrity in a single pass. No separate HMAC step. No room for implementation mistakes.
zk.p4: This isn't security theater. This is the same encryption standard used by intelligence agencies. The difference is we give it to you for free, not for $23/TB/month.

open.title: Open source, because talk is cheap
open.p1: Every cloud provider asks you to trust them. Trust their encryption. Trust their access controls. Trust that the engineer with admin access won't peek at your vacation photos.
open.p2: We don't ask you to trust us. We ask you to read the code.
open.p3: Every line of zcrypt is open source. The encryption implementation. The chunking algorithm. The upload pipeline. The key derivation. If there's a vulnerability, you'll find it before we do, because you have the same access to the source that we do.
open.quote: The best security audit is 10,000 strangers reading your code.

endgame.title: Storage that costs nothing
endgame.p1: A world where personal file storage costs $0 and your data belongs to you.
endgame.p2: Revolutionary? No. Obvious? Yes. Done? Finally.
endgame.p3: The technology for free, encrypted, distributed storage has existed for years. Git hosting has been free for over a decade. AES-256 has been an open standard since 2001. Zstd compression has been open source since 2016. All zcrypt does is connect the dots that the industry had every incentive to leave disconnected.
endgame.p4: Because every dot connected is a revenue stream severed.
endgame.quote: They had every incentive to never build this. So we did.

who.title: The “we” is mostly one guy
who.p1: Honestly? Mostly one guy. I'm Wasif Malik, a full-stack engineer who wanted a lot of free storage, couldn't find any that wouldn't read his files, and got annoyed enough to build the alternative instead of just posting about it. zcrypt is mine end to end: the encryption, the upload pipeline, the drive, and this exact page you're reading.
who.p2: I say “we” out of habit, not to hide behind a logo, and here of all places, that matters. A tool that asks you to trust it with your keys should tell you exactly who wrote the code that holds them. No anonymous founder. No shell company. Just my name, on the record, right here.

sender.s3: Show the QR code or link to the receiver, or read out the code and pairing key

sender.s5: The file and its name are encrypted on your device and relayed as ciphertext

receiver.s1: Scan the QR code, or enter the 6-digit code and pairing key

f1.title: Device to device
f1.desc: Send files between any two devices with a browser. Phone to laptop, laptop to desktop, any combination.

f2.title: End-to-end encrypted
f2.desc: Files and filenames are encrypted with AES-256-GCM on your device. The key is shared by QR code, link or pairing key and never reaches the relay, which only sees ciphertext.

f3.title: Real-time streaming
f3.desc: Files are relayed live over WebSocket as they are encrypted. No waiting for an upload to finish first.

f4.title: Sent in small chunks
f4.desc: The sender encrypts and sends 64 KB chunks, so sending stays light. The receiving browser holds the whole file in memory until it saves, so very large files need a device with room for them.

f5.title: Nothing stored
f5.desc: The relay keeps nothing on disk and forgets the room when the transfer ends. It does see that a transfer happened, its timing and its approximate size.

f6.title: Code, key and confirmation
f6.desc: A 6-digit code finds the room and a separate pairing key (in the QR code or link) encrypts the file. Both screens show the same confirmation code. No accounts, no apps.

verified.title: Verified locally

tieIn.heading: A key the server never sees
tieIn.body: When you protect a folder, its files are re-encrypted under a key derived from a password only you know. That password is verified locally against the folder's own key material. It never travels to the server, and neither does the key it unlocks. Move a file in or out and zcrypt re-keys it for you, so nothing is ever left under the wrong lock.

zk.eyebrow: Decrypted on your device, never on ours
zk.heading: Preview without trusting a server

tieIn.heading: Why we can't read your shares
tieIn.body: A URL fragment (everything after the #) is processed only by the browser and is never included in the request sent to a server. We put the decryption key there on purpose. The server hands over encrypted bytes; the recipient's browser uses the key from the fragment to decrypt them locally. The plaintext never exists on our side.

tieIn.check2: Fragments are never transmitted to the server

server.title: Our servers

guarantees.heading: What we can and can't see
guarantees.subheading: Not a privacy policy promise. A cryptographic one: enforced by where the keys live and what code runs where.

device.title: Encrypted on your device
device.desc: Compression and AES-256-GCM encryption happen in your browser, on your machine, before a single byte goes over the wire.

key.title: Your key never travels
key.desc: Your encryption key is derived from your passphrase on your own device and stays there. It is never sent to us.

unique.title: A unique key per file
unique.desc: Each file gets its own random content key, wrapped by your passphrase key. One file's key can never unlock another.

names.title: Even folder names are sealed
names.desc: File names and folder names are encrypted client-side too. The server can't read your files, their names, or how you organized them.

server.title: The server only sees ciphertext
server.desc: On our side there are no keys and no plaintext: only opaque encrypted blobs we couldn't open even if compelled to.

tamper.title: Tamper-evident by design
tamper.desc: AES-256-GCM authenticates every chunk. If ciphertext is altered in transit or at rest, decryption fails loudly instead of returning garbage.

pipeline.heading: How a file gets sealed
pipeline.subheading: Every upload runs the same four steps, entirely on your device.

derive.title: Derive your key
derive.desc: Your passphrase and a random salt are stretched into a strong key encryption key. This happens locally and the key never leaves your device.

seal.title: Seal each file with its own key
seal.desc: A fresh random content key is generated per file and used to encrypt it. That content key is then wrapped (encrypted) with your passphrase-derived key.

chunk.title: Encrypt folder names, then chunk
chunk.desc: Folder names are encrypted client-side too. The encrypted file is then split into chunks, each individually authenticated.

upload.title: Upload ciphertext only
upload.desc: Only the wrapped key and the encrypted chunks ever leave your device. The server stores blobs it has no way to read.

panel.comment: // what actually lands on the server

tieIn.heading: Lose your passphrase and even we can't recover it
tieIn.body: True zero-knowledge has a price, and we won't pretend otherwise. Because your key is derived from your passphrase and never reaches us, we have no “reset password and get your files back” button. If you lose your passphrase, your data stays encrypted forever: to you and to everyone else.
tieIn.note: That is exactly the property that makes the rest of these promises real. A provider who can recover your files for you can also be compelled to hand them over. We can't do either.
tieIn.panel1: Choose a strong passphrase you won't forget. It is the one key to everything.

resume.title: Resume where it left off

retry.title: Retry on failure

tieIn.heading: No re-encrypting. No re-uploading.

dms.heading: A dead man's switch that reaches a person
dms.body: Choose a trusted contact and a check-in window. If you don't log in for that long, zcrypt emails them a notification. It's a safety net for journalists, activists, and anyone who needs someone alerted if they suddenly can't check in.
dms.does1: Emails a trusted contact you choose if you don't log in for a set window.
dms.does2: Timeout is configurable from 7 to 365 days: you decide the check-in cadence.
dms.does3: Every login automatically resets the countdown, so normal use keeps it quiet.
dms.doesNot1: It does not hand over your files.
dms.doesNot2: It does not release your passphrase or any keys.
dms.doesNot3: It is a heads-up to a person, not an automated handover of access.
dms.footnote: Because zcrypt is zero-knowledge, there are no keys for us to hand over, so the switch alerts a person rather than releasing your data.

snapshots.caveat: Snapshots are manifests for tamper detection, not a restore or version-history system. They don't roll your files back to an earlier state yet.

shared.title: Shared vaults
shared.desc: Collaborate in a vault with other people using viewer, editor, and admin roles.
shared.caveat: The cryptographic key-sharing behind roles is still maturing. Treat shared vaults as experimental and don't rely on them for high-stakes secrets yet.

core.heading: It all sits on the same private core
core.body: Every one of these tools is bounded by the same promise: your files are encrypted on your device with AES-256-GCM before they leave, and we never see your passphrase or your plaintext. The decoy hides a vault we can't read either way; the dead man's switch notifies a person because there are no keys for us to release. Privacy features that can't betray you, because the architecture won't let them.

faq.title: Straight answers
faq.lede: If something's missing, <docs>the docs</docs> have the long version.

0.a: Yes. There are no paid plans and no card. Your files live in accounts you already own, so there's nothing for us to charge for.

1.q: How can there be no limit?
1.a: zcrypt doesn't keep your files. Your connected accounts do. Every account you add is more room, and Telegram has no ceiling at all. New accounts start with 1 GB of shared space while you set things up.

2.a: No. Files are locked on your own device before they're uploaded, and so are their names. We only know where the pieces went, never what's in them.

3.q: What if I forget my password?
3.a: Then nobody can open your files, including us. That's what real privacy costs, so keep it in a password manager.

4.q: Do I need a GitHub or Telegram account?
4.a: Not to start. You can upload right away. Connect an account whenever you want more room. Telegram is the easiest if you already use it.

5.q: Can I share with someone who doesn't use zcrypt?
5.a: Yes. Send them a link. You can add a password, an end date and a download limit, or use Send to make a file that disappears after one read.

6.a: The website does, in Safari. There's no iPhone app yet. There are apps for Mac, Windows, Linux, and Android (beta).

7.q: What if a platform removes my files?
7.a: Then the pieces stored there are gone from there. For anything you can't lose, keep a second copy somewhere else too. That's good advice for every cloud, this one included.

8.q: What happens if zcrypt shuts down?
8.a: Every line of zcrypt is public, so anyone can run it, including you. Once you connect your own accounts, your pieces sit there, not with us. Files in the 1 GB starter space live on a shared account, so if I ever wind it down, I'll say so well ahead of time and you can download everything.

9.a: Every line, under the MIT license. Read it, poke at it, or run the whole thing yourself with docker build and docker run.

2.title: Then it failed at 80 percent

rows.encryption: Encryption model & who holds the keys

z.encryption: AES-256-GCM, keys derived on your device (PBKDF2, 600k iterations). Only you hold them.
z.zeroKnowledge: Yes, by default. File contents are zero-knowledge, and folder and file names are encrypted client-side (a legacy plaintext name column is being retired).
z.storage: Bring your own: GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, or Telegram accounts you already control.
z.free: Free. You supply the storage, so there's no per-gigabyte fee from us.
z.openSource: Fully open source: audit the client and server yourself.
z.folders: Real nestable folders with encrypted folder names and per-folder passwords.
z.previews: Images, video, audio, PDFs, docs, and code: decrypted in your browser, never on the server.
z.sharing: Encrypted share links with expiry. Shared vaults are in beta.
z.lockIn: Minimal. Your data lives in your own accounts and the format is open.

hero.title: Google Drive can read your files. zcrypt can't
hero.lede: Google Drive is deeply integrated and incredibly convenient, but it processes your content for search, previews, and smart features, and it isn't end-to-end encrypted. zcrypt encrypts everything on your device first, stores it in accounts you already own, and is open source from top to bottom.

pillarsHead.title: What changes when nobody else can look

onlyYou.title: Only you can read it
onlyYou.desc: Your passphrase derives the encryption keys on your device with PBKDF2 (600k iterations). Nothing (not search, not smart features, not us) can read your files, because nobody else has the keys.

noScanning.title: No scanning, ever
noScanning.desc: Because content is encrypted with AES-256-GCM before it leaves your device, there's nothing to scan, index, or analyze. The server stores opaque ciphertext, including folder names.

byos.title: Bring your own storage
byos.desc: Connect a GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, or Telegram account you already own. No shared 15 GB pool, no per-gigabyte fees from us, no artificial caps.

openSource.desc: Read the code, audit the crypto, or run the whole thing yourself. How your files are handled isn't a black box.

table.lede: An honest look at where each one fits. Google Drive wins on integration and collaboration; zcrypt wins on privacy, ownership, and openness.

encryption.other: Encrypted in transit and at rest with Google-managed keys. Google can decrypt your files.

zeroKnowledge.other: No. Content is processed for search, previews, smart features, and policy scanning.

storage.other: Google-hosted, pooled across Drive, Gmail, and Photos. Convenient, but you don't own it.

free.other: 15 GB free (shared across Google services); more requires a paid Google One plan.

folders.other: Excellent folders, search, and shared drives, but names and contents are visible to Google.

previews.other: Best-in-class previews and Docs/Sheets editing, generated because Google can read the files.

sharing.other: Very mature sharing and real-time collaboration: at the cost of provider access.

lockIn.other: High. Files, formats, and workflows are tied into the Google ecosystem.

whenBetter.p1: Google Drive is one of the most capable products of its kind, and there are plenty of situations where it's simply the right answer.
whenBetter.p2: If your work revolves around real-time collaboration in Docs, Sheets, and Slides, or you live inside Gmail, Calendar, and the broader Google ecosystem, Drive's integration is unmatched. Multiple people editing the same document live is something an encrypted-at-rest drive fundamentally can't replicate, because that requires the server to read the content.
whenBetter.p3: If you want powerful search across the contents of your files, AI-assisted features, or automatic photo organization, those rely on Google being able to read your data. zcrypt can't offer them precisely because it can't see your files. That's the deliberate trade-off of zero-knowledge.
whenBetter.p4: And if polished native mobile apps are essential today, zcrypt's mobile apps are still on the roadmap. We ship web, desktop, and an Android beta now; Google Drive's mobile apps are mature and complete.
whenBetter.p5: zcrypt is the better fit when you want storage that genuinely can't read your files, lives in accounts you already own, and has nothing hidden behind a proprietary client.

hero.title: Dropbox is convenient. zcrypt is private
hero.lede: Dropbox is a polished, friction-free place to keep files, but it holds the keys and can read what you store. zcrypt is a real encrypted drive where everything is encrypted on your device, stored in accounts you already own, and the code is open for anyone to audit.

pillarsHead.title: What you get that Dropbox won't give you

keys.title: You hold the keys
keys.desc: Your passphrase derives the encryption keys on your device with PBKDF2 (600k iterations). We never see them. Lose the passphrase and even we can't recover your files, that's the point.

locked.title: Locked before it leaves
locked.desc: Files are encrypted with AES-256-GCM before they leave your device. Even folder names are sealed, so the server stores opaque ciphertext and nothing else.

byos.title: Bring your own storage
byos.desc: Point zcrypt at a GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, or Telegram account you already own. No per-gigabyte fees from us, and no artificial caps.

openSource.title: Open source, run it yourself
openSource.desc: Read the code, audit the crypto, or run the whole thing yourself. Nothing about how your files are handled is hidden behind a proprietary client.

table.lede: An honest look at where each one fits. Dropbox wins on polish and ecosystem; zcrypt wins on privacy, ownership, and openness.

encryption.other: Encrypted in transit and at rest, but Dropbox manages the keys and can decrypt your files.

zeroKnowledge.other: No. Dropbox can technically access file contents for previews, search, and scanning.

storage.other: Dropbox-hosted storage on their infrastructure. Simple, but you don't own the backend.

free.other: Limited free tier (a few GB); meaningful capacity requires a paid Plus/Professional plan.

folders.other: Mature, polished folders and sync. Excellent organization, but names are visible to Dropbox.

previews.other: Rich previews and editing, generated server-side because Dropbox can read the files.

sharing.other: Very mature sharing, links, and collaboration: at the cost of provider access.

lockIn.other: Higher. Data and workflows live inside Dropbox's ecosystem.

whenBetter.p1: We're not going to pretend zcrypt wins for everyone. Dropbox is genuinely excellent at what it does, and there are real situations where it's the right tool.
whenBetter.p2: If you need real-time collaborative editing, deep integrations with Office or Google Workspace, or a decade-mature desktop sync client that just works across every device your team owns, Dropbox is hard to beat. Its previews, commenting, and version history are more polished than ours today.
whenBetter.p3: If you specifically want the provider to host and manage storage for you (no accounts to connect, no keys to remember) Dropbox removes that responsibility entirely. With zcrypt, if you lose your passphrase, your data is unrecoverable. That trade-off is the price of zero-knowledge, and it isn't for everyone.
whenBetter.p4: And if you need polished mobile apps today, zcrypt's native mobile apps are still on the roadmap. We ship web, desktop, and an Android beta right now. Dropbox's mobile experience is mature and complete.
whenBetter.p5: zcrypt is the better fit when privacy is non-negotiable: when you want to be the only party who can read your files, keep them in storage you already own, and verify exactly how the encryption works.

hero.title: Both are private. Only one is yours to run
hero.lede: Proton Drive is a genuinely excellent, audited, zero-knowledge drive, and we respect it. The differences are narrower here and more about philosophy: zcrypt is open source and self-hostable, stores files in accounts you already own, and has no artificial caps.

protonDrive.respectNote: Credit where it's due. Proton Drive is end-to-end encrypted, independently audited, backed by an established privacy company, and has mature mobile apps. If you're weighing it against zcrypt, you're already making a privacy-respecting choice. This page is about which trade-offs suit you, not about claiming Proton gets anything wrong.

pillarsHead.title: Where zcrypt goes its own way
pillarsHead.lede: The encryption story is similar. These four things are where zcrypt takes a different path.

openSource.title: Open source, top to bottom
openSource.desc: Like Proton, our apps are open source, and so is the server. You can audit, fork, or run the whole thing. There's no closed component you have to trust on faith.

byos.title: Bring your own storage
byos.desc: This is the big one. Instead of a Proton-hosted quota, point zcrypt at a GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, or Telegram account you already own. No gigabyte caps from us, no separate storage bill.

selfHost.title: Self-host the entire stack
selfHost.desc: Run your own zcrypt server and keep both the keys and the infrastructure under your control. Proton Drive is hosted only. You can't operate your own instance.

table.lede: Both check the privacy boxes. The differences cluster around hosting, storage ownership, and tooling.

encryption.other: End-to-end encrypted with keys derived from your password. Proton can't read your files either.

zeroKnowledge.zcrypt: Yes, by default. File contents are zero-knowledge, and folder and file names are encrypted client-side. Proton is a mature zero-knowledge product that also encrypts file metadata.
zeroKnowledge.other: Yes. Proton Drive is genuinely zero-knowledge and encrypts file metadata as well.

storage.other: Proton-hosted in Swiss/EU data centers. Reputable and managed, but Proton runs the storage.

free.zcrypt: Free. You supply the storage, so capacity isn't metered or sold by the gigabyte.
free.other: Generous free tier; larger storage and bundles require a paid Proton plan.

openSource.zcrypt: Client and server are fully open source.
openSource.other: Proton open-sources its apps and publishes independent security audits.

selfHost.zcrypt: Run the entire stack yourself, client, server, and storage.
selfHost.other: Hosted Proton service only; you can't run your own Proton Drive server.

folders.zcrypt: Real nestable folders with encrypted names, plus optional per-folder passwords.
folders.other: Solid encrypted folders and a clean drive experience.

previews.zcrypt: Images, video, audio, PDFs, docs, and code: decrypted locally in the browser.
previews.other: In-browser previews with client-side decryption, similar approach.

sharing.other: Mature encrypted sharing with password-protected and expiring links.

lockIn.zcrypt: Minimal. Data lives in storage you already own and the format is open.
lockIn.other: Moderate. Your encrypted data lives within Proton's hosted ecosystem.

whenBetter.p1: Proton Drive is a serious, well-built product, and for many people it's the smarter pick. We'd rather you choose the right tool than the one with our name on it.
whenBetter.p2: If you want polished native mobile apps today, Proton has them and zcrypt does not: our mobile apps are still on the roadmap. For people who manage files primarily from a phone, that difference alone may settle it.
whenBetter.p3: If you value a single, fully managed privacy suite (Drive, Mail, Calendar, and VPN under one audited provider in Swiss/EU jurisdiction), Proton delivers that as a cohesive package. zcrypt is focused on being an encrypted drive, not an ecosystem.
whenBetter.p4: If you'd rather not manage your own storage or infrastructure at all, Proton handles everything for you. zcrypt's bring-your-own-storage model is powerful, but it does ask you to connect an account and take responsibility for your passphrase. And some of our more advanced collaboration features, like shared vaults, are still in beta.
whenBetter.p5: zcrypt is the better fit when you want an encrypted drive you can fully self-host, store in accounts you already own, and scale without artificial caps, all open source and free.
